clinicalPearls: Fibrocystic change is the commonest benign breast condition, presenting with lumpy, nodular, often tender breasts that vary with the menstrual cycle, typically in women of reproductive age
Symptoms characteristically worsen in the luteal (premenstrual) phase and improve after menstruation, reflecting hormonal influence on breast tissue
Examination often reveals diffuse nodularity or discrete cysts, most prominent in the upper outer quadrants, sometimes with cyclical mastalgia
It is better regarded as a physiological change than a disease, and most forms carry no increased breast cancer risk; only certain proliferative changes with atypia elevate risk
Assessment follows triple assessment principles, combining clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound in younger women, mammography in older), and needle sampling of any dominant or suspicious lump
A simple cyst confirmed on ultrasound is benign; aspiration is done for symptomatic relief or if the cyst is complex or the fluid is bloodstained
Bloodstained cyst aspirate, a residual mass after aspiration, or a rapidly recurring cyst should prompt further evaluation to exclude malignancy

Management of cyclical breast pain is largely reassurance and supportive measures such as a well-fitting supportive bra and simple analgesia, with reserved use of specific pharmacological agents for severe refractory pain
A new discrete, hard, or fixed lump, or one that does not fluctuate with the cycle, must be investigated rather than attributed to fibrocystic change
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrocystic change reflects an exaggerated but benign response of breast stroma and epithelium to cyclical ovarian hormones. Fluctuating oestrogen and progesterone drive proliferation and involution of the terminal duct-lobular units, producing a spectrum of histological changes including cyst formation, fibrosis (stromal overgrowth), adenosis, and varying degrees of epithelial hyperplasia. Obstruction and dilatation of ducts and lobules generate fluid-filled cysts, while fibrosis produces the palpable nodularity. The hormonal cyclicity explains the premenstrual worsening of pain and swelling and improvement after menstruation.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical breast examination as part of triple assessment
Breast ultrasound, preferred in younger women, to characterise cysts and solid lesions
Mammography in older women or where malignancy is a concern
Fine-needle aspiration or core biopsy of dominant, solid, or suspicious lesions
Cyst aspiration for symptomatic relief and cytology of bloodstained fluid
Histological assessment to identify proliferative change with atypia where relevant to risk
redFlags: A new hard, fixed, or irregular lump, or one that persists after aspiration
Bloodstained cyst aspirate or spontaneous bloody nipple discharge
Rapidly recurring cyst at the same site
Skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or overlying skin change
Axillary lymphadenopathy or a lump that does not vary with the menstrual cycle
Proliferative change with atypia on biopsy indicating elevated cancer risk
reference.prognosis: Fibrocystic change is benign and does not, in its common forms, increase breast cancer risk; symptoms often improve with reassurance and simple measures and tend to settle after the menopause. Cysts may recur but are readily managed. Only the minority with proliferative epithelial change and atypia carry an increased future cancer risk and warrant closer surveillance.
pitfalls: Attributing a new discrete or suspicious lump to fibrocystic change without triple assessment
Ignoring bloodstained aspirate or a residual mass after cyst aspiration
Falsely reassuring a patient by labelling all breast lumpiness as benign disease
Overlooking proliferative atypical changes that do raise cancer risk
Failing to reassess a symptom that does not fluctuate with the menstrual cycle
management: Reassure that fibrocystic change is a benign, hormonally driven physiological process once malignancy is excluded
Complete triple assessment with clinical examination, ultrasound in younger women or mammography in older women, and needle sampling of any dominant or suspicious lump
Give symptomatic relief with a well-supporting bra, simple analgesia and a trial of reduced caffeine where it helps
Aspirate symptomatic or large simple cysts for relief and send any bloodstained fluid for cytology
Manage cyclical mastalgia with topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and, in refractory cases, hormonal agents such as danazol or tamoxifen under specialist guidance
Undertake core biopsy and closer surveillance where proliferative change with atypia is identified given the increased cancer risk
Refer to a breast clinic for any dominant, complex or suspicious lesion
